solution.concept_anchor: Borphukan — Lower Assam frontier governor; Saraighat significance
solution.strong_distractor: b — 'Upper Assam' is the Ahom heartland — students who associate the Borphukan with the most militarily active Ahom officer may assume his post covered the strategic highland core rather than the vulnerable lowland frontier.
elimination_logic: The Borphukan's role was specifically to govern the Mughal-facing frontier — this is why the Borphukan commanded at Saraighat, which is located in lower Assam near Guwahati.
Eliminate option (b): Upper Assam was the Ahom heartland; the Borphukan governed the exposed frontier, which was Lower Assam.
Eliminate option (c): the Borbarua governed the eastern regions/heartland; the Borphukan was the western/Mughal frontier governor.
Eliminate option (d): the Bengal Subah was Mughal territory — the Borphukan administered Ahom territory on the frontier with Bengal.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap exploits the intuition that the most prestigious Ahom military post would cover the kingdom's heartland (Upper Assam). In fact, the Borphukan governed Lower Assam — precisely because it was the dangerous Mughal-facing frontier that required constant military readiness. Lachit's prominence at Saraighat (Guwahati region, Lower Assam) is directly tied to his territorial mandate as Borphukan.
solution.final_explanation:
The Borphukan's territorial charge explains why this office was central to every Mughal-Ahom military confrontation.

• Option (a): CORRECT — The Borphukan was the governor of Lower Assam, the territory that directly bordered Mughal Bengal and faced repeated Mughal military pressure. Guwahati, the site of the Battle of Saraighat, falls within Lower Assam.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Upper Assam was the Ahom heartland where the royal capital (Garhgaon, later Rangpur) was located; different Ahom officials administered that region.
• Option (c): Incorrect — the Borbarua held the combined role of commander-in-chief and chief justice; the Borphukan's charge was specifically the western/lower frontier.
• Option (d): Incorrect — the Bengal Subah was Mughal administrative territory; the Borphukan was an Ahom official governing Ahom territory on the opposite side of the frontier.

Value Addition:
• The Borphukan's dual military-administrative role at the Mughal frontier made it arguably the most operationally important Ahom office during the Mughal conflict period.
• Guwahati (site of Saraighat) sits at the narrowest point of the Brahmaputra valley — its strategic importance as a gateway to Assam explains why it changed hands repeatedly.
• The five Patra Mantris collectively governed distinct territorial and functional domains — the Borphukan's assignment to the frontier reflects the kingdom's geopolitical threat assessment.

statement_analysis.statement: Ram Singh I, the Mughal commander at the Battle of Saraighat, was a Rajput nobleman — the son of Mirza Raja Jai Singh — appointed by Aurangzeb to recover Guwahati from Ahom control.
statement_analysis.reason: Ram Singh I's Rajput identity and lineage (son of Mirza Raja Jai Singh, who had negotiated with Shivaji) are documented; his appointment to recover Guwahati after Mir Jumla's withdrawal is historically accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: Beyond military operations, Ram Singh I attempted diplomatic overtures and is documented in Buranji accounts to have tried to bribe Ahom commanders — revealing a Mughal strategy that combined force with subversion.
statement_analysis.reason: Buranji accounts record Ram Singh's attempts to negotiate and bribe Ahom officers, reflecting a dual-track Mughal approach; this also reveals the Mughal intelligence assessment that Ahom unity might be fracturable.

statement_analysis.statement: Ram Singh I and Mirza Raja Jai Singh are the same historical individual — 'Ram Singh' being the Hindu name and 'Mirza Raja Jai Singh' the Mughal honorific for the same person.
statement_analysis.reason: Ram Singh I and Mirza Raja Jai Singh are father and son, not the same person. Jai Singh commanded the Deccan campaign against Shivaji (1665); Ram Singh I commanded the Assam campaign (1671). Conflating them is the most common error regarding this lineage.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know the father-son relationship but are unsure of the roles may accept Statement 3 as a possible interpretation of 'same lineage = same person' and select (d) — all three correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 3 explicitly equates Ram Singh I with Mirza Raja Jai Singh as a single person — this is factually wrong; they are father and son; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statement 1 accurately describes Ram Singh I's lineage and mission — correct.
Statement 2 accurately describes the diplomatic-bribery strategy recorded in Buranjis — correct.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap between Ram Singh I and his father Mirza Raja Jai Singh is one of the most sophisticated traps in Mughal-Ahom history. Both are Rajput military commanders in Mughal service with similar names and connected historical periods. Statement 3 exploits this confusion by offering a plausible-sounding 'dual-naming' explanation. A student who knows both figures but has not clearly separated their roles will find Statement 3 ambiguous rather than definitively wrong.
solution.final_explanation:
Ram Singh I's Saraighat campaign illustrates the Mughal approach of combining military force with diplomatic subversion.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Ram Singh I was a Rajput commander, son of Mirza Raja Jai Singh, appointed by Aurangzeb after Mir Jumla's failure to consolidate Mughal gains in Assam. His Rajput identity is historically noted — a Hindu commanding Mughal forces against predominantly Hindu Ahoms.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Buranji accounts record Ram Singh's diplomatic overtures and attempted bribery of Ahom commanders. This dual military-diplomatic strategy reveals the Mughal recognition that the Ahoms could not be defeated easily by military means alone.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Ram Singh I and Mirza Raja Jai Singh are father and son — distinct historical figures. Jai Singh is associated with the Treaty of Purandar (1665) with Shivaji; Ram Singh I commanded at Saraighat (1671). Conflating them is the primary error this question targets.

Value Addition:
• The Ahom counter-intelligence reportedly detected Ram Singh's bribery attempts — recorded as a testament to Ahom command cohesion.
• Ram Singh I reportedly wrote to Aurangzeb that he could not defeat the Ahoms — a dispatch preserved in Mughal records alongside the Buranji account.
• The deployment of a Hindu Rajput against the Ahoms reflects Aurangzeb's pragmatic (rather than religiously motivated) military appointments in this theatre.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may correctly identify A-1 (Charaideo-first capital) and D-4 (maidams-burial) but then swap B and C — matching Khelniyals with king-making power (confusing them with great nobles) and Burhagohain/Borgohain with Khel administration.

D-4 is secure: Maidams are burial mounds for Ahom royalty — directly paired with 'royal mortuary tradition.'

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets B and C — Khelniyals and the great nobles (Burhagohain/Borgohain). The trap is refined: 'intermediaries between state and paiks' (Khelniyals) vs. 'hereditary king-making authority' (great nobles) requires precise functional knowledge, not just name recognition.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests cross-concept knowledge of Ahom institutions across founding, administration, nobility, and cultural practice.

Correct matches:
• A–1: Charaideo was Sukapha's first capital, established c.1253 CE near present-day Sivasagar — its foundational status is unambiguous.

• C–3: The Burhagohain and Borgohain held hereditary, constitutionally recognized authority to elect and depose the swargadeo — the most powerful check on royal absolutism in the Ahom system.

Trap: B-3 and C-2 is the typical error — confusing Khelniyals with the great nobles' king-making function.

Value Addition:
• The five Patra Mantris (great nobles) and the Khel system operated at different levels — nobles at the constitutional apex, Khelniyals at the functional administrative base.
• Charaideo retains spiritual significance for the Tai-Ahom community even today — annual Maidams-puja ceremonies are conducted there.

solution.concept_anchor: Turbak Khan's 1532 invasion — defeated by Suhungmung
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who associate the Ahom-Mughal conflict primarily with the Saraighat period may attribute the 1532 victory to a post-Akbar Mughal context and confuse Suhungmung with Chakradhwaj Singha (the Saraighat-era king).
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Chakradhwaj Singha was the Ahom king associated with the Saraighat period (1671), not the 1532 invasion.
Eliminate option (b): Sukapha was the founder (1228 CE) — Turbak Khan's invasion in 1532 falls three centuries later.
Eliminate option (d): Lachit Borphukan was a military commander, not the Ahom king, and lived in the 17th century.
Option (c): Suhungmung (also known as Dihingia Raja) was the Ahom king who repelled Turbak Khan's invasion in 1532 — the correct pairing.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap conflates two periods of Ahom military success — the 1532 victory against Turbak Khan and the 1671 victory at Saraighat. Students who have studied the Saraighat period in depth may attribute the earlier 1532 victory to the more famous Saraighat-era leaders (Chakradhwaj Singha or Lachit Borphukan). The obscurity of Suhungmung's name compared to Lachit's fame is the trap's engine.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ahom kingdom's military resistance to Muslim incursions predates the Mughal consolidation period.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Chakradhwaj Singha was the Ahom king associated with rebuilding military strength after the humiliation of Ghilajharighat (1663) and initiating the Saraighat campaign — 17th century, not 1532.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Sukapha was the 13th-century founder; Turbak Khan's invasion in 1532 falls outside his reign by three centuries.
• Option (c): CORRECT — Suhungmung (c.1497–1539) defeated Turbak Khan's invasion in 1532. This pre-Mughal consolidation victory is an important but often neglected data point in Ahom military history.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Lachit Borphukan was a 17th-century military commander (Borphukan, not king); his association with Ahom military glory leads students to incorrectly attribute earlier victories to his name.

Value Addition:
• Turbak Khan's 1532 invasion predates Humayun's second Afghan war — it represents an independent Afghan/pre-Mughal incursion into Ahom territory.
• Suhungmung's reign also saw the expansion of Ahom territory and consolidation of the Paik system.
• The Ahom military record before Saraighat includes this often-overlooked 1532 victory — demonstrating that Ahom resistance was not a sudden 17th-century phenomenon.

solution.concept_anchor: Shankardev movement — Sattra autonomy vs. Ahom state tension

statement_analysis.statement: Srimanta Shankardev's Ekasharana Dharma movement transcended caste boundaries in Ahom-ruled Assam, attracting both high-caste and low-caste devotees through its emphasis on single-minded devotion to the divine.
statement_analysis.reason: Ekasharana Dharma's egalitarian theology — rejecting Brahmin ritual monopoly and caste hierarchy — is historically documented and represents one of its defining social features.

statement_analysis.statement: The Sattra institutions established under Shankardev's influence functioned throughout Ahom history as subordinate extensions of the royal court, receiving consistent patronage from all Ahom kings without exception.
statement_analysis.reason: Sattras developed as autonomous parallel power centers that sometimes created political tension with the Ahom state; not all Ahom kings patronized the movement — the relationship was ambivalent and sometimes hostile.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who associate Vaishnavism with Ahom royal patronage (a partially true narrative) may accept Statement 2 as correct without noting 'consistent' and 'all Ahom kings without exception' — the scope-extension qualifiers that make it false.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Ekasharana Dharma's cross-caste appeal is a well-documented historical feature — Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: 'Consistent patronage from all Ahom kings without exception' and 'subordinate extensions of the royal court' — both are false absolute claims; some kings were hostile and Sattras were autonomous, not subordinate; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c). Re-checking options: (a)=both correct, (b)=both incorrect, (c)=S1 correct S2 incorrect, (d)=S1 incorrect S2 correct. Correct_option = c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates through two qualifiers in Statement 2: 'consistent patronage' and 'all Ahom kings without exception.' Each qualifier makes the statement false — some kings actively opposed the Sattra movement, and Sattras were autonomous institutions, not royal extensions. A student who knows 'Ahom kings patronized Vaishnavism' without examining these qualifiers will accept Statement 2 as broadly true.
solution.final_explanation:
The Shankardev-Ahom state relationship reveals the complexity of religion-state interaction in medieval India.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Ekasharana Dharma explicitly welcomed devotees irrespective of caste — a radical social position that attracted broad following across Ahom society. The movement's cultural output (Borgeet, Ankiya Naat) reflects this inclusive ethos.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The relationship between Ahom kings and the Sattra institutions was not uniform or consistently supportive. Some kings patronized; others were hostile or indifferent. Sattras grew into autonomous centers of religious, cultural, and economic power — parallel to, and sometimes in tension with, royal authority. They were not subordinate extensions of the court.

Value Addition:
• Shankardev reportedly faced opposition from both Brahmin orthodoxy and certain Ahom rulers during his lifetime (c.1449–1568).
• The Sattra system survives today as living institutions in Assam with significant landholdings and cultural authority — their autonomy is a historical continuity.
• The Ahom patronage of Vaishnavism was part of the broader Hinduization process but did not eliminate Tai-Ahom ethnic practices — a key nuance for examination questions.

solution.concept_anchor: Ahom-Mughal revenue system contrasts — non-monetized vs. cash-based

statement_analysis.statement: The early Ahom state extracted its primary economic resource through compulsory labor and military service rather than through monetary land revenue assessments.
statement_analysis.reason: The non-monetized, service-based character of the Paik system is a defining feature of early Ahom administration, contrasting with contemporary Mughal revenue in cash/kind.

statement_analysis.statement: Bhogdekhi land grants in the Ahom system were functionally identical to Mughal jagirs — both involved revenue-farming rights assigned to nobles and military commanders.
statement_analysis.reason: Bhogdekhi grants were made to religious institutions and nobles within a non-monetized economy without revenue-farming rights; Mughal jagirs were cash-revenue assignments within a monetized system. Their economic contexts and mechanisms are fundamentally different.

statement_analysis.statement: The gradual monetization of the Ahom economy under later kings introduced social tensions that the earlier service-based system had largely avoided.
statement_analysis.reason: Historical accounts indicate that monetization disrupted existing social arrangements — paiks who had cultivated land under the service system faced new pressures as cash demands were introduced.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike the Ahom Paik system, Mughal mansabdars received transferable jagirs whose revenue yield was not tied to their personal labor or military service to the empire.
statement_analysis.reason: Mughal mansabdars were assigned jagirs based on rank (mansab), not labor — they extracted revenue from assigned territories through agents. The contrast with paik service obligation is structural and fundamental.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Bhogdekhi grants existed and that jagirs also involved noble grants may accept Statement 2 as correct (seeing both as 'noble grants') and count three correct items, selecting option (b).
elimination_logic: Statement 2 equates Bhogdekhi grants with Mughal jagirs as 'revenue-farming rights' — Bhogdekhi had no revenue-farming mechanism in a non-monetized economy; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statements 1, 3, and 4 each accurately describe documented features of Ahom-Mughal revenue contrasts — all three are correct.
Three of four correct → option (a) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's partial-truth trap acknowledges that both Bhogdekhi and jagir involved state grants to individuals/institutions — which is true. But the critical distinction is economic mechanism: Bhogdekhi grants operated in a non-monetized service economy without revenue-farming rights, while jagirs were revenue-farming assignments in a cash economy. Students who recall only the surface similarity (both are grants) without the economic mechanism difference will accept Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ahom-Mughal revenue comparison is a high-frequency topic requiring precise differentiation of mechanisms, not just labels.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Paik system's service-extraction logic stands in direct contrast to Mughal cash/kind revenue assessment — this is the foundational economic difference between the two systems.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Bhogdekhi grants ≠ Mughal jagirs. Bhogdekhi lands were granted to religious bodies/nobles without revenue-farming rights, in an economy that did not operate on cash assessments. Mughal jagirs were transferable revenue assignments within a monetized fiscal framework.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Monetization under later Ahom kings disrupted the stable service-cultivation balance of the Paik system — a social consequence with historical documentation.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Mughal mansabdars extracted revenue through agents from assigned territories — the opposite of the paik's personal service obligation.

Value Addition:
• Revenue-farming (jagir) requires monetization — without cash flow, revenue cannot be farmed. This structural point explains why jagir-like arrangements did not develop within the early Ahom economy.
• The Mughal jagirdari system's crisis under Aurangzeb (too many mansabdars, insufficient jagir land) has no parallel in the Ahom service-based system.
• Land grants in both systems (Bhogdekhi and nisboi in Ahom; madad-i-maash in Mughal) served ideological legitimacy functions even if their economic mechanisms differed.

solution.concept_anchor: Ahom fall — Burmese not Mughal; Treaty of Yandabo 1826
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Ahom kingdom did not fall to Mughal power; the effective end of Ahom sovereignty came through Burmese invasions (1817–22) followed by British annexation under the Treaty of Yandabo (1826).

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. The Treaty of Yandabo (1826) was not a bilateral agreement between the Ahoms and the British; it was a treaty between the British East India Company and Burma (after the First Anglo-Burmese War), by which Burma ceded Assam to British India. The Ahoms were not a party to this treaty — they had already lost sovereignty to Burma before the British arrived.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect (mischaracterizing Yandabo as an Ahom-British treaty rather than a Burma-British treaty), the answer is (c) — A correct, R incorrect.
A correct + R incorrect → correct_option is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation/factual trap in R exploits the common simplification that 'the British took over Assam through the Treaty of Yandabo.' This is partially true but imprecisely stated — the treaty was between the British and Burma, not the British and the Ahoms. Students who know the treaty name and its outcome (Assam to British) but not its parties will accept R as correct, gravitating toward option (a) or (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The precise sequence of Ahom sovereignty's end is critical for accurate examination answers.

Assertion (A): Correct — The Mughals never permanently annexed Ahom territory despite repeated military campaigns. The Ahom kingdom fell to Burmese invasions (1817–22), and British India subsequently acquired Assam not through conquest of the Ahoms but through the Treaty of Yandabo.

Reason (R): Incorrect — The Treaty of Yandabo (1826) was concluded between the British East India Company and Burma, ending the First Anglo-Burmese War. Burma ceded Assam (which it had occupied) to the British. The Ahoms were not a party to this treaty. Describing it as an 'agreement between the Ahoms and the British East India Company' misidentifies both the context and the parties.

Since A is correct and R is factually wrong, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• The Treaty of Yandabo also resulted in Burma ceding Arakan and Tenasserim and paying a war indemnity to the British.
• The Burmese occupation of Assam (1817–26) is remembered as the 'Manmaria' period — characterized by widespread depopulation and devastation.
• Assam's British acquisition through a Burma-Britain treaty (not direct conquest) is a distinctive feature of northeastern Indian colonial history.

statement_analysis.reason: The Ahoms were a Tai-speaking ruling minority; the broader Assamese identity is a composite that developed through centuries of cultural synthesis. Equating 'Ahom' with 'Assamese' as an immediate identity is anachronistic and ethnically imprecise.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students may accept Statement 3 as plausible ('alliances as fallback after failed conquest' sounds historically realistic) and reject it only with precise knowledge of Sukapha's documented strategy.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses an entity-swap of causation — attributing the alliance strategy to military failure rather than design. This sounds plausible because political accommodation as a post-conflict strategy is a common historical pattern. The UPSC trap exploits generic plausibility over specific historical knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The origin and identity questions around the Ahom kingdom require precision about ethnic distinctions and foundational strategies.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Tai-Ahom and Shan people both belong to the broad Tai family but are ethnically and historically distinct — the Ahoms' migration narrative from Yunnan/Southeast Asia is specific to their sub-group.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Ahom-Assamese identity distinction is one of the most important conceptual points in Ahom history. The Ahoms were a Tai-speaking ruling minority; modern Assamese identity is a composite product of centuries of synthesis — not an immediate equivalence.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Sukapha's alliance and assimilation policy is documented as deliberate design, not a response to military failure. The alliances with Moran, Matak, and Bodo peoples were the foundational state-building strategy — marriages, shared governance, and cultural incorporation were the primary instruments.

Value Addition:
• The Tai-Ahom linguistic heritage is preserved in Buranji literature and in Ahom religious ceremonies still practiced in Assam.
• The Moran, Matak, and Bodo peoples retain distinct identities in present-day Assam — their historical incorporation into the Ahom state is a formative moment in regional ethnogenesis.
• 'Assamese identity' as a composite category emerged through the Ahom period — understanding this synthesis is essential for northeastern Indian history questions.

solution.concept_anchor: Ahom military success — terrain, logistics, not weaponry or numbers

statement_analysis.statement: The Ahom military's consistent success against Mughal forces was primarily attributable to their possession of superior firearms and artillery, which outmatched the Mughal military-technological complex.
statement_analysis.reason: Ahom military success was not based on superior weaponry — the Mughals had significantly better artillery. Ahom success derived from terrain mastery, riverine warfare, guerrilla tactics, and logistical disruption of Mughal supply lines.

statement_analysis.statement: The Brahmaputra river system served as a strategic asset for the Ahoms, enabling their river craft fleet to neutralize the Mughal cavalry's numerical advantage in the riverine terrain of lower Assam.
statement_analysis.reason: The Brahmaputra's riverine geography was the decisive strategic factor — Mughal cavalry effectiveness was severely reduced in marshy, waterlogged terrain, while Ahom boat fleets controlled river access and flanking routes.

statement_analysis.statement: Lachit Borphukan's tactical innovations at Saraighat included exclusively conventional frontal naval assaults, demonstrating that the Ahoms had abandoned guerrilla tactics in favour of set-piece battles by the 1671 campaign.
statement_analysis.reason: Lachit employed a combination of tactics — cutting supply lines, using island fortifications, encircling the Mughal fleet, and fighting personally to inspire troops. The battle involved both riverine positional warfare and asymmetric disruption, not exclusive frontal assaults.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Statement 1 is wrong (no superior weapons) but accept Statement 3 as describing 'naval battle = conventional frontal assault' will select option (b) — '1 only' is NOT correct — missing that Statement 3 is also incorrect.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 'superior firearms and artillery' is the explicit claim — Mughals had better artillery; Ahom success was terrain and logistics, not weapons; Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2: Brahmaputra as strategic asset neutralizing Mughal cavalry — historically accurate; Statement 2 is correct, not an answer to 'NOT correct.'

Statement 3: 'exclusively conventional frontal naval assaults' and 'abandoned guerrilla tactics' — Lachit used multiple tactics including supply-line interdiction and island fortifications; Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are both NOT correct → option (a) 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 3 uses 'exclusively' — a qualifier that converts a partially true observation (Saraighat involved set-piece naval engagement) into a false absolute claim. Students who know Saraighat was a formal naval battle may miss the guerrilla-logistics dimension that Lachit simultaneously employed, accepting Statement 3 as broadly correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Ahom military success is one of the most conceptually important examination topics — requiring understanding of why, not just that, the Ahoms resisted the Mughals.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Ahom military success was never based on superior weaponry. The Mughals had significantly better artillery (the Mughal 'gunpowder empire' advantage). Ahom victory derived from riverine terrain mastery, guerrilla logistics, and asymmetric tactics — not weapons parity or superiority.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Brahmaputra's geography was the equalizing strategic factor. Mughal cavalry — their primary military arm — was neutralized in marshy, waterlogged terrain where boats ruled. The Noukha Khel's institutional boat-building capacity gave the Ahoms a decisive riverine edge.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Lachit's tactics were multi-layered — cutting Mughal supply lines at key river crossings, using island fortifications as defensive pivots, and personally leading from his boat when his forces wavered. 'Exclusively frontal assaults' misrepresents the tactical sophistication of the Saraighat campaign.

Value Addition:
• The phrase 'superior use of terrain and logistics' rather than 'superior weaponry' is the conceptually correct framing for Ahom military success.
• Island fortifications on the Brahmaputra gave the Ahoms defensible nodes that Mughal forces could not easily assault without naval superiority.
• Lachit's multi-pronged approach — combining psychological leadership, supply interdiction, and direct naval engagement — anticipates modern asymmetric warfare doctrine.
